### Introduction
The problem of automatic speech recognition has recently attracted researchers in all fields of knowledge. One of the most interesting applications of automatic speech recognition is the automatic call routing in call centers. Call routing is usually classified into two categories; static and dynamic. In static call routing, the routing of calls to agents is based on a predefined routing strategy. The caller selects an option and is transferred to an agent in the corresponding department. In dynamic call routing, routing rules are applied to determine the optimal assignment of calls to agents. With dynamic call routing the transfer of the caller to an agent of a department is not predetermined. The problem of automatic speech routing has been widely studied in the literature (Narasimhan and Bhat, 2001; Yang et al, 2007; Varga and Kocsor, 2007; Boulis et al, 2007; Varga, 2009; Hasegawa-Johnson and Schultz, 2010). However, most of the authors have proposed call routing algorithms based on static routing or have not used speech recognition. In this article we deal with dynamic call routing and also have used speech recognition as a pre-processing step of call routing.
Dynamic call routing is an important issue because call routing should be done in real time. Abstract:
Purpose – As a major part of the built environment, the role of the service provider in the building has become an important issue in the literature. Facilities management (FM) companies have been responsible for the management and operations of the building, and are now providing integrated management of the building. They play an increasingly pivotal role in building performance and sustainability. This paper aims to explore the changing role of the service provider from a sustainable FM perspective.Design/methodology/approach – This is a conceptual paper that is based on previous literature of the development of FM service delivery process and on the new concept of sustainability. A holistic process of FM services is proposed based on the sustainability approach to the built environment. The FM service processes were identified and an analytical model was developed that links the service provision with sustainability. Findings – Three service processes were identified and developed in terms of the service providers' activities: maintenance, technical, and user support service. The sustainability concept was then applied to the processes. Sustainability indicators were added to the FM service processes. The proposed FM service process model was analysed and discussed.

## Introduction
Inorganic pigment layer was traditionally prepared by pigmenting a layer of inorganic pigment and polymer on the surface of a paperboard with a thin film of polymer resin in a press. Since inorganic pigment layer has a porous structure, the mechanical strength of the layer is typically weak, as can be seen from the fact that inorganic pigment layer is separated easily from the paperboard by tapping the color block (ref. 1, 2). In addition, inorganic pigment layer is characterized by highly porous structure that absorbs water when it is wetted, resulting in considerable shrinkage and/or warpage in the color block. Also due to the low water vapor resistivity of inorganic pigment layer, the color block easily loses its mechanical strength when it is exposed to the atmospheric conditions. Therefore, an effective means of improving mechanical strength and decolorization resistance of inorganic pigment layer should be developed.
Among the various methods for improving mechanical strength and decolorization resistance of the color block, the method that uses liquid additive seems to be promising (ref. 3). In this method, a carboxylated styrene-butadiene copolymer liquid is added to the formulation of the inorganic pigment layer in order to improve the water vapor resistivity of the pigment layer, resulting in enhancement of decolorization resistance. Furthermore, due to the densification of the pigment layer caused by incorporation of a liquid additive, which will be presented in the next section, the resulting color block is expected to have less warpage and/or shrinkage. ### Introduction: Family Values
Family values are the ethical beliefs and principles of the family. Traditionally, they serve as the moral compass guiding the daily lives of families and include norms such as love, loyalty, respect, honesty, responsibility, sharing, and reciprocity. In general, family values represent what parents want their children to believe and do. Although the values that families hold are not necessarily unique, it is assumed that they are shared and that family members agree on the importance of those values to the functioning of the family. Historically, family values have been transmitted and reinforced from one generation to the next. The role of children in family life and in the community is to assist in the transmission of family values through interaction with parents, grandparents, siblings, extended family, and neighbors. Family values can be communicated and shared through various means, including through play, through activities and traditions, and through the use of family rituals. For example, family rituals or routines such as family dinners and celebrations promote family connectedness, which in turn supports positive values.
With globalization and the growing influence of technology, there is concern that family values are declining. Many researchers, including Sroufe and Schork (1989), have demonstrated the adverse effects on young people of a loss of family values and norms, which is associated with increases in risk taking, poor academic achievement, and delinquency. Furthermore, when parents focus on the achievement of their children in school, on material possessions, or on individual interests to the exclusion of family values, there is a weakening of the value of the family as an institution and of the intergenerational transmission of family values.

The research community is now beginning to turn to the use of gene trap and conditional targeted knockout models. Such models allow us to test whether loss of a defined signaling pathway has any effect on a particular cell-type response. In the long term these models will facilitate the identification of the downstream genes that act as specific readouts for particular signaling pathways. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of all patients presenting with symptomatic ICAD to a regional tertiary-care stroke center during a 5 year period. We analyzed demographic and comorbid data, as well as admission and discharge medications. Subgroup analyses were performed to determine whether there was a relationship between age and sex and the frequency of AMM.
Results: 133 patients presenting with symptomatic ICAD were included. Of these, 88% were AMM at discharge, 76% of whom received clopidogrel, and 88% received high-dose statin. Of those discharged on AMM, only 57% received antiplatelet therapy for greater than or equal to 6 months post-stroke. No significant differences in the use of AMM was observed between older (≥80 years old) and younger (<80 years old) patients (95% vs. 83%, p = 0.15) or between men and women (90% vs. 79%, p = 0.30).
Conclusions: Despite limited evidence for the benefits of AMM, this practice is being widely applied in contemporary clinical practice for patients with symptomatic ICAD. Future research is needed to establish whether this practice is a best practice or a practice to be avoided.
